title: Resumption, interception & suspend edge cases
scopeHtml: Scope: where a coroutine resumes and who decides, ContinuationInterceptor, suspendCoroutine as the low-level primitive, suspend function types and lambdas, calling suspend from Java, ThreadLocal across suspension, stack traces and recovery basics, per-suspension allocation cost, and blocking or locking across suspension points.

questions.promptHtml: After a coroutine suspends, which thread does it resume on? Is it guaranteed to come back to the same thread?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many developers think of a coroutine as "a lightweight thread". The interviewer wants to see that you understand a coroutine is a chain of continuations, and that the dispatcher in its context picks the thread each time it resumes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A coroutine does not own a thread. When it suspends, its state is saved in a continuation object and the thread is released. When something later calls resume, the continuation goes through the ContinuationInterceptor in the coroutine's context, which is normally a CoroutineDispatcher, and that dispatcher decides where the rest of the code runs. On Dispatchers.Main that means the main thread. On Dispatchers.Default or IO it means any thread in the pool, which may differ from the one before the suspension. Only a single-threaded dispatcher guarantees the same thread. With Dispatchers.Unconfined, or with no interceptor at all, the code continues on whatever thread called resume.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A suspend function is compiled into a state machine (chunk 13 covers the CPS details). At a suspension point, the function stores its locals into its continuation object and returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED all the way up the call stack. At that point the thread is free and runs other work. Nothing about the coroutine stays on the thread's stack.

Later, some other code calls continuation.resumeWith(result). That could be a timer, an OkHttp callback thread, a Binder thread, or another coroutine. What happens next depends on which continuation object was resumed. The library never hands out the raw state-machine continuation. It hands out an intercepted one:

suspending code in coroutine C (context = Job + Dispatchers.IO)
   |
   | suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont -> ... }   // cont wraps c.intercepted()
   v
intercepted() --> context[ContinuationInterceptor].interceptContinuation(c)
                   = DispatchedContinuation(dispatcher = IO, continuation = c)

some thread T later calls cont.resume(value)
   |
   v
DispatchedContinuation.resumeWith:
   if dispatcher.isDispatchNeeded(context) -> dispatcher.dispatch(context, this)   // hop to a pool thread
   else                                    -> run c.resumeWith(value) right here on T

So the rule is: the resuming thread is whatever the dispatcher in the coroutine's context picks at the moment of resumption. It is not the thread the coroutine was on before. Concretely:

Context dispatcher Where code after a suspension point runs
Dispatchers.Main Main thread, always posted via Handler
Dispatchers.Main.immediate Main thread; runs inline if resume is already called on main
Dispatchers.Default Any Default worker; may be a different thread each time
Dispatchers.IO Any thread from the shared pool; may differ each time
single-thread executor dispatcher, limitedParallelism(1) newSingleThreadContext / single-thread executor: the same thread. limitedParallelism(1): one at a time, but not necessarily the same physical thread
Dispatchers.Unconfined Whatever thread called resume
no interceptor (raw startCoroutine with EmptyCoroutineContext) Whatever thread called resume

Note the limitedParallelism(1) row. It guarantees serial execution, not thread affinity. Its tasks run on the underlying pool's threads one at a time. This matters if you use it to guard thread-affine resources such as a ThreadLocal, a SQLite connection bound to a thread, or an OpenGL context.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun demo() = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    println("before: ${Thread.currentThread().name}")   // DefaultDispatcher-worker-3
    delay(10)                                           // suspends, thread released
    println("after:  ${Thread.currentThread().name}")   // may be DefaultDispatcher-worker-7
}

// Broken assumption: thread identity used as a key
val perThreadBuffer = ThreadLocal<StringBuilder>()
suspend fun appendLog(msg: String) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    val sb = perThreadBuffer.get() ?: StringBuilder().also(perThreadBuffer::set)
    sb.append(msg)
    delay(5)                 // may resume on another worker
    sb.append(" done")       // fine, same local `sb`...
    perThreadBuffer.get()    // ...but this may be a DIFFERENT buffer, or null
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming that withContext(Dispatchers.IO) pins you to one thread for the whole block. It pins you to one pool.
  • Using Thread.currentThread(), ThreadLocals, or thread-bound resources across a suspension point. See Q270 for the fix.
  • Thinking limitedParallelism(1) gives thread affinity. It gives mutual exclusion only.
  • Forgetting that the code inside a callback-based suspendCancellableCoroutine block runs on the current thread, while the code after it runs wherever the dispatcher sends it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who actually calls resume? → Whatever completes the operation: a timer for delay, a network callback thread, another coroutine that sends to a channel, or a Handler message. The library's intercepted wrapper then re-dispatches.
  2. Does a coroutine that never suspends ever change thread? → No. Without a real suspension, everything runs on the starting thread. A suspend call that returns its value immediately does not dispatch.
  3. Why does Dispatchers.Main.immediate sometimes run code synchronously? → Its isDispatchNeeded returns false when you are already on the main looper, so the resume runs inline. That is why viewModelScope uses it: it avoids a frame of latency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "it resumes on the dispatcher". The senior explains the mechanism: intercepted() wraps the continuation, isDispatchNeeded controls inline vs posted resumption, Unconfined and the no-interceptor case run on the resumer's thread, and limitedParallelism(1) is serial but not thread-affine. They also tie this to concrete thread-affinity bugs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team used limitedParallelism(1) to wrap a native SDK whose handles were bound to the thread that created them. It passed in tests and crashed intermittently in production once the IO pool grew and tasks landed on different workers. The fix was a real single-thread executor dispatcher.

questions.promptHtml: What is a suspend function type like suspend () -> Unit, and why can you call delay() inside list.forEach { } but not inside Thread { } or a Runnable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you understand that "suspendability" is part of a function's type and depends on the call site, rather than a magic keyword. It also checks whether you know how inlining affects that.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: suspend () -> T is its own function type. A value of that type can only be invoked from a coroutine or another suspend function, because the compiler passes it a hidden Continuation. A regular () -> T lambda body is not a suspend context, so suspend calls inside it don't compile. The exception is lambdas passed to inline functions such as forEach, map, and let. Their bodies are inlined into the enclosing suspend function, so a suspend call inside them is really a suspend call in your function. Thread { } and Runnable take non-inline lambdas that run later on another stack, so suspension is impossible there.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Type-level fact: suspend () -> Int on the JVM is a function that takes an extra Continuation<Int> and returns Any?, which is either the value or COROUTINE_SUSPENDED. It is not a subtype of () -> Int, and () -> Int is not a subtype of it. They are different shapes.
  • Conversions the compiler allows:
    • A lambda literal in a position expecting a suspend type becomes a suspend lambda: val f: suspend () -> Unit = { delay(1) }.
    • A non-suspend function reference or value can be converted to a suspend function type ("suspend conversion"). It is supported for callable references since Kotlin 1.4, and for general function-typed expressions in later 1.x versions. A non-suspend function trivially "never suspends", so this is safe.
    • The reverse, suspend to non-suspend, is never allowed. The suspend function has nowhere to send its continuation.
  • Where suspend calls are legal: inside a suspend function body, a suspend lambda body, or the body of a lambda that is inlined into one of those (and is not marked crossinline/noinline in a way that puts it into another object).
  • Receivers: launch takes block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit, a suspend lambda with receiver. That is why this inside launch { } is a CoroutineScope and why you can call launch again inside it.
suspend fun load() {                     // has a Continuation
   items.forEach { delay(10) }           // inline -> body pasted into load(): OK
   items.asSequence().map { delay(10) }  // Sequence.map is NOT inline -> compile error
   Thread { delay(10) }                  // Runnable lambda, not inline -> compile error
   val r = Runnable { runBlocking { delay(10) } }  // compiles, but now blocks that thread
}

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Accepting suspend work as a parameter
suspend fun <T> retrying(times: Int, block: suspend () -> T): T {
    repeat(times - 1) {
        try { return block() } catch (e: IOException) { delay(200) }
    }
    return block()
}

// Non-suspend reference passed where a suspend type is expected: allowed (suspend conversion)
fun readCached(): String = "cached"
suspend fun use() = retrying(3, ::readCached)

// Broken: callback API with a non-inline lambda
fun interface OnDone { fun done() }
fun legacyAsync(cb: OnDone) { /* ... */ }

suspend fun broken() {
    legacyAsync { delay(100) }   // ERROR: suspension functions can be called only within coroutine body
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Fixing" the compile error with runBlocking { } or GlobalScope.launch { } inside the callback. The first blocks the callback thread. The second detaches the work from structured concurrency. The right fix is to bridge the callback with suspendCancellableCoroutine or callbackFlow (chunk 23).
  • Expecting Sequence operators to accept suspend lambdas. They are not inline. Use Flow or a plain loop.
  • Marking a lambda parameter crossinline in your own inline function and then being surprised that suspend calls inside it are rejected when it's invoked from an object or another lambda context.
  • Declaring an API parameter as () -> T when callers will need suspend work. Callers can always pass non-suspend code to a suspend parameter, so prefer suspend () -> T when the callee is already suspend.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a fun interface have a suspend method? → Kotlin 1.4 did not allow it; later versions do. Verify on your compiler version. For most code a plain suspend function type is simpler.
  2. What's the type of ::someSuspendFun? → A KSuspendFunctionN. You can pass it wherever suspend (..) -> R is expected.
  3. Why is suspend not allowed on a property getter? → Property access has no call-site syntax that signals suspension. Use a suspend function, or expose a Flow.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer stops at "you need to be in a coroutine". The senior explains that suspend is part of the type, why inline lambdas are allowed (code is pasted into the caller's state machine), which way conversions go, and how to bridge non-inline callback lambdas correctly instead of reaching for runBlocking.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A common review finding is runBlocking inside an OkHttp Interceptor or a Runnable that someone wrote to get around this compile error. It shows up later as an ANR or as thread-pool starvation.

questions.contextHtml:
A photo-gallery app has 1.2M DAU and 60% of its users are on low-end devices (2-4 GB RAM). Release 5.3 moved thumbnail loading from AsyncTask to coroutines. The user-perceived ANR rate went from 0.21% to 0.68%, above Play's 0.47% bad-behavior threshold. The new code:

class ThumbRepository(private val resolver: ContentResolver) {
    suspend fun loadThumb(uri: Uri, size: Int): Bitmap {
        val opts = BitmapFactory.Options().apply { inSampleSize = 4 }
        return resolver.openInputStream(uri)!!.use { BitmapFactory.decodeStream(it, null, opts)!! }
    }
}
class GalleryViewModel(private val repo: ThumbRepository) : ViewModel() {
    fun onBind(uri: Uri) = viewModelScope.launch { _thumbs.update { it + (uri to repo.loadThumb(uri, 256)) } }
}

ANR traces show main in BitmapFactory.nativeDecodeStream under ThumbRepository.loadThumb, which is under DispatchedTask.run and Handler.handleCallback. The same release also upgraded the image library and enabled a new GC config, and the Crashlytics breadcrumbs mention GC pauses. The author says "it's a suspend function, so it's async".
questions.promptHtml: What's wrong, how do you fix it, and how do you stop it from happening again?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Suspend functions run in the background, so maybe the GC change is the problem," or "Wrap it in GlobalScope.launch." Both miss the point that suspend adds no thread switch, and the second just leaks work.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Are all the ANR stacks in decode, or are some in GC or lock waits? This tells me whether the GC lead is real.
    • Which dispatcher does viewModelScope use here? It uses Dispatchers.Main.immediate, which confirms we're on main.
    • How many binds per second happen during a fling? This sizes the work: at roughly 30 binds per second and 15-40 ms per decode on low-end devices, main is busy for 450-1200 ms of every second.
    • Was the old AsyncTask path running on a background executor? It was, which explains why this is a regression.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that wraps the body in withContext(Dispatchers.IO), or behind a remote flag fall back to the old loader. Halt the staged rollout of 5.3 while the fix bakes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. A blocking decode runs on main because a suspend function without a context switch runs on the caller's dispatcher. This is strongly supported by the stack: Handler.handleCallback under DispatchedTask.run is the main dispatcher running our continuation.
    2. Too many concurrent decodes once moved off main. This is not the cause yet, but it becomes relevant after the fix.
    3. GC pauses from the new config. This is a red herring unless traces show main waiting in GC. GC can make ANRs worse but would not put nativeDecodeStream on main.
    4. The image library upgrade. It is unrelated to this code path, since we call BitmapFactory directly.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Read the ANR traces in Play Console.
    • Record a Perfetto trace of a fast fling on a low-end device and look for long decodeStream slices on the main thread track.
    • Turn on StrictMode detectDiskReads() in debug builds. It flags openInputStream on main immediately.
    • Log Thread.currentThread().name inside loadThumb in a debug build.
  5. Root cause: suspend only means "this function may suspend". The compiler adds a continuation parameter and nothing else. Code in a suspend function runs on whatever thread called it until it hits a real suspension point that dispatches elsewhere. loadThumb has no suspension point at all. openInputStream and decodeStream are blocking calls, so the whole decode runs synchronously on the main thread under viewModelScope's Main.immediate.
  6. Fix: Short-term: make the function main-safe itself, following the convention that a suspend function is safe to call from main. 
    class ThumbRepository(
    private val resolver: ContentResolver,
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO,
) {
    suspend fun loadThumb(uri: Uri, size: Int): Bitmap = withContext(io) {
        val opts = BitmapFactory.Options().apply { inSampleSize = 4 }
        resolver.openInputStream(uri)?.use { BitmapFactory.decodeStream(it, null, opts) }
            ?: error("decode failed for $uri")
    }
}
    Long-term: bound decode concurrency, for example with Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4) or a Semaphore (dispatcher and sync choices are owned by chunks 16 and 21). Cancel on unbind with a per-item Job so fast flings don't queue hundreds of decodes. Better still, use the image library with proper inSampleSize computed from the bounds and caching.
  7. Prevention:
    • StrictMode thread policy with penaltyLog/penaltyDeath in debug builds and CI UI tests.
    • A review checklist rule: "every suspend function that does blocking IO/CPU must switch context inside itself".
    • A Detekt/lint rule that flags known blocking calls (BitmapFactory.decode*, InputStream.read, Thread.sleep) in suspend functions that have no withContext.
    • An ANR-rate alert per staged rollout cohort.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I would not switch the ViewModel's scope to Dispatchers.IO (viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) at every call site). It pushes the responsibility onto every caller and someone will forget it.
    • I would not use GlobalScope, because it loses cancellation.
    • I would not add yield() calls. A single native decode cannot be split.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Would Dispatchers.Default be better?" → Decode is mostly CPU, so Default is defensible. But openInputStream on a content URI can block on IPC and disk. I'd keep IO or split the work: read on IO, decode on Default. The important point is moving it off main, and the choice between pools is second-order.
  • "Is the !! a problem too?" → Yes. openInputStream can return null, and decode returns null on a corrupt file. Inside launch on viewModelScope that throws an NPE that crashes the app (exception handling is chunk 19). Handle null explicitly.
  • "Why didn't a unit test catch this?" → Tests with runTest and fakes never touch real decode. Main-safety is about threads, so it shows up in StrictMode, instrumented tests, or a Perfetto trace, not in JVM tests.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: In one migration, a dozen repository methods were converted to suspend by adding the keyword, and none of them switched context. Their ANR rate doubled across three releases before anyone connected the dots. The fix was mechanical. The real win was a lint rule plus StrictMode in the debug flavour, which caught four more cases in the following quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes suspend implies a background thread, or blames GC without reading the stack.
  • Hire: identifies main-thread blocking from the stack, fixes it with withContext(Dispatchers.IO) inside the repository, and mentions main-safety.
  • Strong hire: also bounds concurrency, cancels on unbind, sets up StrictMode, lint, and rollout monitoring, and dismisses the red herrings with reasoning.

questions.promptHtml: What is ContinuationInterceptor, and how does CoroutineDispatcher use it to control where a coroutine runs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who use dispatchers from people who know what a dispatcher is. The mechanism explains Main.immediate, Unconfined, why custom dispatchers work, and why the context's interceptor is special.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ContinuationInterceptor is a CoroutineContext.Element from the Kotlin standard library with one main job: wrap a continuation before it's resumed. Its interceptContinuation(c) method returns a new continuation that can redirect the resume. CoroutineDispatcher implements it by returning a DispatchedContinuation. When that is resumed, it asks isDispatchNeeded(context). If the answer is yes, it calls dispatch(context, runnable) to run the rest of the coroutine on its threads. If the answer is no, it runs inline. There can be only one interceptor per context, because it's keyed by ContinuationInterceptor.Key, so adding a dispatcher replaces the previous one.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Standard library interface (kotlin.coroutines):

public interface ContinuationInterceptor : CoroutineContext.Element {
    companion object Key : CoroutineContext.Key<ContinuationInterceptor>
    public fun <T> interceptContinuation(continuation: Continuation<T>): Continuation<T>
    public fun releaseInterceptedContinuation(continuation: Continuation<*>) { }
}

The flow inside the compiled code and the library:

1. Compiled state machine: ContinuationImpl (one per suspend-function invocation)
       intercepted(): Continuation<Any?>
         = cached ?: context[ContinuationInterceptor]?.interceptContinuation(this) ?: this
         (cached in the ContinuationImpl's `intercepted` field)

2. Library suspension primitives (suspendCancellableCoroutine, delay, Channel, Mutex ...)
       always resume `uCont.intercepted()`, never the raw state machine

3. CoroutineDispatcher.interceptContinuation(c) = DispatchedContinuation(this, c)

4. DispatchedContinuation.resumeWith(result):
       if (dispatcher.isDispatchNeeded(context)) dispatcher.dispatch(context, this)   // this is a Runnable/Task
       else run inline (via a thread-local event loop to avoid unbounded recursion)

5. When the ContinuationImpl completes -> releaseIntercepted() -> interceptor.releaseInterceptedContinuation(...)

Key properties:

  • Single slot. Dispatchers.IO + Dispatchers.Main yields Main, because the right side wins for the same key. Every dispatcher shares the ContinuationInterceptor key. Since kotlinx.coroutines 1.x, CoroutineDispatcher also has a polymorphic key so context[CoroutineDispatcher] works.
  • The interceptor sees resumptions, not individual suspend calls. A suspend function that returns without suspending never touches it.
  • withContext(newDispatcher) changes the interceptor for the block. When the block finishes, the outer coroutine resumes through its own interceptor. That is how you "come back" to Main.
  • isDispatchNeeded is the knob. Dispatchers.Unconfined returns false (always inline). Main.immediate returns false only when already on the main looper. Most others return true.
  • Interceptors are not only dispatchers. Test frameworks and some tracing tools wrap continuations. Kotlinx test dispatchers are dispatchers too; they enqueue onto a virtual-time scheduler.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// A logging interceptor that delegates to a real dispatcher (illustrative, not for production)
class LoggingDispatcher(private val delegate: CoroutineDispatcher) : CoroutineDispatcher() {
    override fun isDispatchNeeded(context: CoroutineContext) = delegate.isDispatchNeeded(context)
    override fun dispatch(context: CoroutineContext, block: Runnable) {
        val name = context[CoroutineName]?.name ?: "?"
        delegate.dispatch(context) {
            Log.d("Dispatch", "resume $name on ${Thread.currentThread().name}")
            block.run()
        }
    }
}

// Trap: two dispatchers in one context — the last one wins, silently
val ctx = Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("sync") + Dispatchers.Default
check(ctx[ContinuationInterceptor] === Dispatchers.Default)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking a dispatcher "owns" coroutines. It only receives Runnables to run. It has no knowledge of the coroutine beyond its context.
  • Writing a custom ContinuationInterceptor that is not a CoroutineDispatcher and using it with kotlinx.coroutines. Many library internals (withContext fast paths, yield, delay) rely on CoroutineDispatcher behaviour, so wrap or extend a dispatcher instead.
  • Implementing dispatch so that it runs the block inline. The API docs recommend signalling inline execution through isDispatchNeeded == false rather than running the block in place inside dispatch. That way the library can use its event loop. Running inline in dispatch can cause stack overflows and reentrancy bugs.
  • Forgetting that Dispatchers.Unconfined and Main.immediate change when code after a resume runs, which affects ordering assumptions (see Q273).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does yield() do in terms of the interceptor? → It checks for cancellation and, if the dispatcher's isDispatchNeeded is true, dispatches the continuation to the back of the queue, giving other tasks a turn. On Unconfined it behaves differently (it is mostly a no-op unless an event loop is running).
  2. Why does withContext sometimes not dispatch at all? → If the new context's dispatcher equals the current one, it takes a fast path and runs the block without a dispatch. It only creates a new Job boundary.
  3. How would you make every coroutine in a scope run through a tracer without changing call sites? → Put a wrapping dispatcher in the scope's context, as above, or better, use a ThreadContextElement (Q270) which gets callbacks on every resume and suspend without changing threading.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "a dispatcher decides the thread". The senior names interceptContinuation, the cached intercepted(), DispatchedContinuation, isDispatchNeeded vs dispatch, the single-key replacement rule, and the consequences for ordering and testing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A home-grown "MainThreadInterceptor" that ran blocks inline when already on main (instead of overriding isDispatchNeeded) caused recursive resumption. A chain of 2,000 nested emissions produced a StackOverflowError on older devices.

questions.promptHtml: Every suspending API eventually bottoms out in something like suspendCoroutine. How does it actually work? What happens if resume is called before the block returns, or called twice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is the one place you can see suspension with no magic. Knowing it shows you understand the "return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED or a value" protocol, and it explains real bugs: the synchronous-resume fast path and double resume.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: suspendCoroutine { cont -> ... } hands my lambda a continuation for "the rest of this function" and suspends until someone resumes it. It is built on the compiler intrinsic suspendCoroutineUninterceptedOrReturn. It wraps the intercepted continuation in a SafeContinuation, runs my block on the current thread, then calls getOrThrow(). If my block already called resume synchronously, getOrThrow returns the value and nothing suspends. If not, it returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED and the thread is released. Resuming a second time throws IllegalStateException("Already resumed"). Plain suspendCoroutine does not react to cancellation. In production code I use suspendCancellableCoroutine (compared in chunk 23).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The stdlib implementation (simplified, current Kotlin 2.x):

public suspend inline fun <T> suspendCoroutine(crossinline block: (Continuation<T>) -> Unit): T {
    return suspendCoroutineUninterceptedOrReturn { c: Continuation<T> ->
        val safe = SafeContinuation(c.intercepted())
        block(safe)
        safe.getOrThrow()
    }
}
  • suspendCoroutineUninterceptedOrReturn is an intrinsic. The compiler replaces it with "give me my own continuation c and let the lambda's return value be my return value". If the lambda returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, the state machine returns that marker and unwinds. Otherwise the value is the result.
  • c.intercepted() means that when someone resumes, the dispatcher in the context gets to choose the thread (Q263, Q266).
  • SafeContinuation is a tiny atomic state machine:
state: UNDECIDED --resume(v) before getOrThrow--> RESUMED(v) --getOrThrow--> returns v (no suspension)
       UNDECIDED --getOrThrow first-------------> SUSPENDED  --resume(v)--> delegate.resumeWith(v) (dispatch)
       RESUMED / already handed off --resume again--> IllegalStateException("Already resumed")

That synchronous fast path is important. Many callback APIs call the callback immediately if the data is cached. Without SafeContinuation, that would resume a function that hasn't finished suspending yet, which corrupts the stack.

  • Exceptions: cont.resumeWithException(e) makes e be thrown from the suspension point in the coroutine. If the block itself throws before resuming, the exception propagates out of suspendCoroutine directly.
  • Never resumed: the coroutine stays suspended forever. Plain suspendCoroutine doesn't hook cancellation, so cancelling the Job doesn't wake it. The enclosing scope then can't complete, and anything captured stays in memory. This is the big reason to prefer suspendCancellableCoroutine.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Minimal bridge (illustrative): ok for an API that always calls back exactly once
suspend fun Prefs.readAsync(key: String): String? = suspendCoroutine { cont ->
    readInBackground(key) { value, error ->
        if (error != null) cont.resumeWithException(error) else cont.resume(value)
    }
}

// Bug 1: API calls back twice (onSuccess then onComplete) -> IllegalStateException: Already resumed
suspend fun broken(): Result = suspendCoroutine { cont ->
    sdk.start(object : Listener {
        override fun onSuccess(r: Result) = cont.resume(r)
        override fun onComplete(r: Result) = cont.resume(r)   // second resume crashes
    })
}

// Bug 2: callback never fires on error path -> coroutine hangs forever, ignores cancel
suspend fun hangs(): Data = suspendCoroutine { cont ->
    sdk.fetch { data -> if (data != null) cont.resume(data) /* else: nothing */ }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming code inside the block runs "in the background". It runs synchronously on the current thread, before the suspension. Heavy work there blocks the caller.
  • Storing the continuation in a field and resuming it from multiple places without a guard. Use one resume path, or if (cont.isActive) with a cancellable continuation.
  • Expecting Job.cancel() to unblock a suspendCoroutine. It won't.
  • Swallowing errors by never resuming on the failure path. It hangs instead of failing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the lambda crossinline? → It's executed inside the intrinsic's lambda, a different context, so non-local returns from it must be forbidden.
  2. Is the Continuation thread-safe to resume from any thread? → Yes. The SafeContinuation CAS handles the race with getOrThrow, and the intercepted wrapper dispatches to the right thread.
  3. How does delay() relate to this? → delay uses suspendCancellableCoroutine, a cancellable cousin of this primitive. It asks the dispatcher (or the default event loop) to call resume after the timeout, which on Android Main means Handler.postDelayed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "it turns a callback into a suspend function". The senior explains the intrinsic, the UNDECIDED/RESUMED/SUSPENDED race, the synchronous fast path, the double-resume exception, and why non-cancellable suspension leaks. They also mention which variant they'd actually ship.
