sections.html: A payment SDK fired both onSuccess and onFinished, and wrapping it in suspendCoroutine produced an "Already resumed" crash in about 0.3% of checkouts. That is exactly the double-resume path in the state diagram above.

questions.promptHtml: How is a suspend lambda like the block in launch { } compiled, and how does the library actually start running it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It connects the language feature (suspend lambdas) to the library (launch), and shows that kotlinx.coroutines is "just a library" built on a few stdlib intrinsics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A suspend lambda compiles to a class that extends the stdlib's internal SuspendLambda. That class is both the lambda object and its own continuation/state machine. Its invokeSuspend method holds the body as a label-based state machine, and create() makes a fresh instance bound to a completion continuation. The stdlib provides createCoroutine and startCoroutine on suspend function types. launch uses the unintercepted variant: it creates the coroutine with the StandaloneCoroutine/Job as completion, intercepts it with the context's dispatcher, and resumes it with Unit. That first resume either dispatches to a thread or, with UNDISPATCHED, runs immediately.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
launch(context) { body }
   |
   | newContext = scope.coroutineContext + context (+ Default if no dispatcher)
   | coroutine  = StandaloneCoroutine(newContext)    // Job + Continuation<Unit> (the "completion")
   | start(CoroutineStart.DEFAULT, coroutine, block)
   v
block.createCoroutineUnintercepted(receiver = coroutine, completion = coroutine)
   -> calls the generated lambda class's create(receiver, completion)  // new state-machine instance, label = 0
   .intercepted()                                                       // DispatchedContinuation via dispatcher
   .resumeCancellableWith(Result.success(Unit))                         // first "resume" = start
   -> dispatcher.dispatch(...) -> later: invokeSuspend(Unit) runs the body from label 0
   -> when the body finishes: completion.resumeWith(result) -> Job completes, parent notified

What the compiler generates for scope.launch { val a = repo.a(); val b = repo.b(a); show(b) } (roughly):

Piece Purpose
class X$1 : SuspendLambda, Function2<CoroutineScope, Continuation<Unit>, Any?> the lambda object
fields label, L$0 (spilled a), captured vars state across suspension points
create(value, completion) fresh instance per coroutine start
invoke(scope, cont) create(scope, cont).invokeSuspend(Unit) (direct invocation path)
invokeSuspend(result) when(label) state machine body

Notes on versions: Kotlin 2.0 switched regular lambdas to invokedynamic (LambdaMetafactory) generation by default. Suspend lambdas still compile to generated classes, because they need to be their own continuation with fields for spilled state. Check decompiled bytecode on your toolchain if this matters for method counts.

Stdlib entry points (kotlin.coroutines), all real:

  • (suspend () -> T).createCoroutine(completion): Continuation<Unit>. It creates the coroutine but doesn't start it. The returned continuation is intercepted.
  • (suspend () -> T).startCoroutine(completion). It creates and resumes immediately in the current thread until the first suspension.
  • Receiver variants for suspend R.() -> T.
  • kotlin.coroutines.intrinsics.createCoroutineUnintercepted. The library uses this, then intercepts explicitly so it can choose the start mode.

CoroutineStart (full treatment in chunk 15) just picks how that first resume happens: DEFAULT dispatches, UNDISPATCHED resumes inline until the first suspension, LAZY stores the continuation until start()/join(), and ATOMIC dispatches but can't be cancelled before it starts.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Running a coroutine with zero kotlinx.coroutines: shows the stdlib is enough
fun <T> runNaked(block: suspend () -> T, onDone: (Result<T>) -> Unit) {
    block.startCoroutine(Continuation(EmptyCoroutineContext) { result -> onDone(result) })
}
// No interceptor in EmptyCoroutineContext -> code after each suspension resumes on whoever calls resume.

// A suspend lambda value is invoked like any function, but only from suspend code
val fetch: suspend (String) -> User = { id -> api.user(id) }
suspend fun load() = fetch("42")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing the lambda instance passed to launch is reused between starts. Each start calls create, so captured mutable objects are shared, but the per-run state (label and spilled locals) is fresh.
  • Capturing a large object (Activity, View) in a suspend lambda that is stored for later (LAZY start, or retry wrappers). The lambda class holds a strong reference until the coroutine completes.
  • Thinking startCoroutine is "asynchronous". It runs on the current thread until the first suspension, with no dispatcher unless the context has one.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does launch take suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit rather than suspend () -> Unit? → So the body has a CoroutineScope receiver: the new coroutine itself. Child launch/async calls inside it automatically become children.
  2. What's RestrictedSuspendLambda? → The class used for lambdas whose receiver type is annotated @RestrictsSuspension, for example sequence { } builders. They can only call the receiver's own suspend members, never arbitrary suspend functions like delay.
  3. If suspend lambdas are classes, what's the method-count and APK impact of hundreds of launch { } blocks? → Each produces a class with a few methods. R8 shrinks and merges, but it's real DEX weight. It rarely matters next to resources, but it is one reason not to wrap every one-liner in its own coroutine.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "the compiler makes a state machine". The senior describes SuspendLambda, create/invokeSuspend, the stdlib createCoroutine/startCoroutine intrinsics, how launch wires completion to the Job and interception to the dispatcher, and the Kotlin 2.0 indy nuance for regular vs suspend lambdas.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A retry helper stored suspend () -> T blocks in a queue to replay later. Those lambdas captured a Fragment through requireContext() and kept it alive after navigation. LeakCanary pointed at a generated ...$1 suspend-lambda class as the GC root path.

questions.promptHtml: What does a Kotlin suspend fun look like from Java, and what are the realistic ways for Java code to call it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most Android codebases with real history still have Java modules, Java SDK consumers, or Java tests. This question checks whether you understand the compiled signature, and whether you can pick a bridge without blocking threads or breaking cancellation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: From Java, suspend fun user(id: String): User becomes Object user(String id, Continuation<? super User> $completion). It takes an extra Continuation parameter, returns Object, and returns either the result or the COROUTINE_SUSPENDED marker. Java can technically implement Continuation by hand, but that's fragile. In practice I add a Kotlin-side adapter: one that returns a CompletableFuture via scope.future { } (in kotlinx-coroutines-core since 1.7, needs API 24+ on Android), a Guava ListenableFuture via kotlinx-coroutines-guava, an Rx type via the rx3 bridge, or a plain callback plus a cancel handle. runBlocking works but blocks the calling thread, so it's acceptable only off the main thread, in tests or tooling.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Compiled shape (decompile any suspend function to confirm):

// Kotlin
suspend fun user(id: String): User
// JVM signature
public final Object user(String id, Continuation<? super User> $completion)
// Return value: User | COROUTINE_SUSPENDED (IntrinsicsKt.getCOROUTINE_SUSPENDED())

Why hand-implementing Continuation in Java is a trap:

  1. You must handle both return paths: an immediate value from the return, and later delivery via resumeWith. Many people only handle one.
  2. resumeWith receives a Result that is an inline class. From Java it shows up as an Object that is either the value or an internal Result.Failure, which is awkward and not public API.
  3. You must provide a CoroutineContext. Without a Job there is no cancellation, and without a dispatcher you resume on whatever thread finished the work.
  4. There is no structured concurrency. Nobody cancels the work when the Java caller goes away.

Bridges, compared:

Bridge Artifact / version Cancellation Notes
scope.future { } → CompletableFuture<T> kotlinx-coroutines-core (jdk8 module merged in 1.7) future.cancel(true) cancels the coroutine CompletableFuture needs Android API 24+
scope.future { } → ListenableFuture<T> kotlinx-coroutines-guava cancel() propagates Works on all API levels; Guava's listenablefuture dependency
rxSingle { } / rxCompletable { } kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 Disposing cancels Good if the consumer already uses RxJava
Callback + Cancellable handle your own facade You wire job.cancel() Zero extra deps, most Java-idiomatic on old API levels
runBlocking { } core Thread interrupt does not cancel nicely Blocks a thread; never on main

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Kotlin facade for Java callers
class UserRepositoryJava(
    private val repo: UserRepository,
    private val scope: CoroutineScope,   // owned by the caller/SDK, e.g. SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate
) {
    // API 24+: CompletableFuture
    fun userAsync(id: String): CompletableFuture<User> = scope.future { repo.user(id) }

    // Any API level: callback + cancel handle
    fun interface Callback<T> { fun onResult(value: T?, error: Throwable?) }
    fun interface Cancellable { fun cancel() }

    fun user(id: String, cb: Callback<User>): Cancellable {
        val job = scope.launch {
            val result = runCatching { repo.user(id) }
            if (result.exceptionOrNull() is CancellationException) return@launch // don't report cancel as error
            cb.onResult(result.getOrNull(), result.exceptionOrNull())
        }
        return Cancellable { job.cancel() }
    }
}
// Java caller
Cancellable handle = facade.user("42", (user, error) -> { /* main thread if scope uses Main */ });
// onDestroy: handle.cancel();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping in runBlocking and calling it from a Java Activity, which causes an instant ANR risk. Or calling it from an OkHttp interceptor, which causes thread starvation.
  • Using GlobalScope.future { } in the facade, so the work can never be cancelled when the screen dies.
  • Using CompletableFuture in a library whose minSdk is below 24. Core library desugaring does not reliably cover CompletableFuture for every consumer, so check before relying on it.
  • Reporting CancellationException to Java callbacks as a failure. Java callers then show error toasts on normal navigation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you write a JUnit test in Java for a suspend function? → Call a small Kotlin test helper that uses runTest. Or, if you must, use BuildersKt.runBlocking(...) from Java. The Kotlin helper is cleaner.
  2. Can Java implement a Kotlin interface that has suspend members? → Technically yes, by implementing the Object m(..., Continuation) shape, but it's very error-prone. Provide an abstract Kotlin adapter class that exposes a callback- or future-based method for Java to override.
  3. Is there an annotation that auto-generates blocking bridges? → Not in the official toolchain. Third-party compiler plugins exist, but they generate blocking wrappers, which is the wrong default on Android. Explicit facades are better.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "use runBlocking or a callback." The senior shows the compiled signature and why hand-rolled continuations break, and picks a bridge by API level, existing deps, and cancellation semantics. They give ownership of the scope to the caller or SDK lifecycle, and filter out CancellationException.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Java-heavy module called a Kotlin repository through a runBlocking helper "temporarily". Months later the helper was being called from a click handler, and the ANR traces pointed at BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking on main.

questions.promptHtml: Why do ThreadLocals break with coroutines, and how does ThreadLocal.asContextElement() fix it? What can still go wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Logging MDC, tracing spans, request IDs, locale overrides and legacy SDK "current session" globals often live in ThreadLocals. Moving to coroutines silently breaks them. Interviewers want the mechanism and the remaining sharp edges.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A ThreadLocal is bound to a thread, but a coroutine can resume on a different thread after each suspension, and other coroutines run on "its" thread in between. So reading a ThreadLocal after a suspension gives you some other coroutine's value, or none. tl.asContextElement(value) creates a ThreadContextElement. It sets the ThreadLocal to value every time the coroutine starts or resumes on any thread, and restores the thread's previous value when the coroutine suspends or completes. The catch: calling tl.set() inside the coroutine is not persisted across suspensions. To change the value you need withContext(tl.asContextElement(newValue)). And code that isn't running inside such a coroutine sees whatever the thread had, so use ensurePresent() to fail fast.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Thread W1                 Thread W2
coroutine A (rid=A) runs
A suspends  -----------\
coroutine B (rid=B) runs \
                          \--> A resumes on W2
                               tl.get() == ?    <- without context element: W2's value (stale / B's / null)
                                                <- with asContextElement:   "A" (set on resume)

ThreadContextElement<S> has two hooks that kotlinx.coroutines calls on every transition:

  • updateThreadContext(context): S runs right before the coroutine's code runs on a thread (start and every resume). It returns the previous thread state.
  • restoreThreadContext(context, oldState: S) runs right after the code yields that thread (suspension or completion).

asContextElement is the ready-made implementation for a ThreadLocal. Its default value is get() at creation time, so tl.asContextElement() captures the current thread's value when you build the context.

Helpers (all real, kotlinx.coroutines core):

  • ThreadLocal.isPresent() (suspend) tells you whether the element for this ThreadLocal is in the current coroutine context.
  • ThreadLocal.ensurePresent() (suspend) throws IllegalStateException if it isn't. Useful to assert "this code must run with a request ID".

Ecosystem examples: kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j's MDCContext() for logging MDC (more common server-side), and OpenTelemetry's Kotlin extension for propagating its Context. Both are built on ThreadContextElement.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val requestId = ThreadLocal<String?>()

fun handle(scope: CoroutineScope, id: String) = scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO + requestId.asContextElement(id)) {
    log("start ${requestId.get()}")  // id
    delay(50)                        // may resume on another worker
    log("after ${requestId.get()}")  // still id: the element re-applied it on resume

    requestId.set("changed")         // BROKEN: lost at the next suspension/resume
    delay(1)
    log(requestId.get())             // back to id, not "changed"

    withContext(requestId.asContextElement("child")) {   // CORRECT way to change it
        log(requestId.get())         // child
    }
    log(requestId.get())             // id again
}

suspend fun mustHaveRequestId(): String {
    requestId.ensurePresent()        // ISE if called from a coroutine without the element
    return requestId.get()!!
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using tl.asContextElement() (no argument) on a thread where the value isn't set yet. That captures null, and the coroutine faithfully re-applies null.
  • Expecting a child coroutine to see tl.set() changes made by its parent. Children inherit the element (the value at element creation), not the live ThreadLocal.
  • Assuming the thread is "clean" outside coroutines. Code that runs on a pool thread outside any coroutine sees whatever was last left there. There are also reported edge cases around undispatched/Main.immediate execution (kotlinx.coroutines issue #4121) where a value is visible longer than expected. Don't build security decisions on ThreadLocals.
  • Putting a mutable object in the ThreadLocal and mutating it from parallel children. The element shares the same object across all of them, which is a data race.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's the per-resume cost? → Two calls per thread hop (update and restore). For a ThreadLocal that's a get plus a set, which is cheap. A custom element that allocates on every resume can show up in hot loops.
  2. Can I write my own element, for example to push or pop a tracing span? → Yes, implement ThreadContextElement<S> with updateThreadContext/restoreThreadContext. CopyableThreadContextElement (experimental, added in the 1.6 line; check the opt-in on your version) also lets you customize what children inherit via copyForChild/mergeForChild.
  3. Does Android's Trace.beginSection work across suspension? → No. It is per-thread and must end on the same thread. For async spans across suspension use Trace.beginAsyncSection/endAsyncSection (API 29+) or androidx.tracing's equivalents, and call them in the coroutine code, not as a ThreadLocal.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "use asContextElement". The senior explains the update/restore hooks on every resume and suspend, why set() doesn't stick, inheritance semantics, ensurePresent, the shared-mutable-object race, and when to replace ThreadLocals altogether with explicit parameters or context elements of their own.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a coroutine migration, analytics events started carrying the wrong sessionId about 2% of the time. The legacy tracker read it from a ThreadLocal, and IO workers were serving several sessions in turn. Scenario Q276 walks through that incident.

questions.promptHtml: Why are exception stack traces from coroutines often useless, and what does kotlinx.coroutines' stack-trace recovery do about it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every team that moves to coroutines hits Crashlytics reports that end in BaseContinuationImpl.resumeWith with no caller. A senior should explain why (stackless coroutines) and what the library can and can't recover. Deep debugging tooling belongs to chunk 32; this question is about the basics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Coroutines are stackless. When a coroutine suspends, the call stack unwinds completely, and on resume the thread stack starts from the dispatcher's run loop: DispatchedTask.run → resumeWith → invokeSuspend. So an exception's trace shows only the frames since the last resume, not who called the function in the first place. Stack-trace recovery is a debug-mode feature on the JVM. When an exception crosses a coroutine boundary, for example via await() or withContext, the library copies it and appends the receiving coroutine's frames, keeping the original as the cause. It is on by default only in debug mode: -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug, or JVM assertions enabled. On Android, assertions are effectively off, so you must set the property yourself, typically only in debug builds.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
What a raw trace looks like when fetchProfile() fails after a suspension:

java.io.IOException: HTTP 503
    at com.app.data.ProfileApi.fetchProfile(ProfileApi.kt:41)
    at com.app.data.ProfileApi$fetchProfile$1.invokeSuspend(ProfileApi.kt)
    at kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.BaseContinuationImpl.resumeWith(ContinuationImpl.kt:33)
    at kotlinx.coroutines.DispatchedTask.run(DispatchedTask.kt:...)
    at kotlinx.coroutines.scheduling.CoroutineScheduler$Worker.run(...)
    // missing: which ViewModel / use case called fetchProfile

The logical callers (ProfileRepository.load → ProfileViewModel.refresh) are not on the thread stack. They exist only as a chain of continuation objects in the heap, linked through completion references.

How recovery works (JVM, debug mode):

  1. Each compiled continuation class carries @DebugMetadata (source file, line numbers per label, method name). The library uses it to turn the continuation chain into synthetic stack frames.
  2. When an exception is rethrown in another coroutine, the library tries to create a copy of the same exception type with the original as cause, then writes the reconstructed frames into the copy. Places include Deferred.await, withContext returning, Channel.receive, and Job.join failures surfacing.
  3. Copying uses a public constructor that takes a message, a cause, both, or no arguments. kotlinx.coroutines has long offered CopyableThrowable<T> (experimental) for custom copying. Current kotlinlang docs also describe a stdlib StackTraceRecoverable interface (experimental opt-in). Check which one your versions support. If no way to copy is found, the original is thrown unchanged.
  4. Recent versions mark the join point with a synthetic boundary frame (shown as _COROUTINE._BOUNDARY) so you can see where the coroutine hop happened.

Enabling it on Android (debug builds only):

class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) System.setProperty("kotlinx.coroutines.debug", "on")  // before any coroutine runs
        super.onCreate()
    }
}

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Trap: identity changes when recovery is on
val original = IOException("boom")
val d = scope.async { throw original }
try { d.await() } catch (e: IOException) {
    println(e === original)        // false in debug mode (a copy), true otherwise
    println(e.cause === original)  // true in debug mode
}

// Exception that cannot be auto-copied: no (message)/(cause)/() constructor
class ApiError(val code: Int) : Exception("api $code")   // recovery silently skipped

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Comparing exceptions by identity (===) or using exception instances as sentinels. Recovery breaks that in debug builds and tests, because JVM unit tests usually run with assertions enabled.
  • Assuming recovery helps production Crashlytics. It is debug-mode only and costs reflection plus allocations per rethrow. Most teams leave it off in release.
  • Custom exceptions with only non-standard constructors, such as an error-code-only constructor. They won't be enriched. Add a (message, cause) constructor or a copy hook.
  • R8 can remove "unused" constructors that recovery would call reflectively. Then recovery silently doesn't happen in minified debug builds. Keep rules may be needed if you depend on it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What helps in production, where recovery is off? → CoroutineName in contexts, logging at boundaries (repository/use-case catch, wrap, and rethrow with context), breadcrumbs, and structured error types that carry the operation name. Chunk 32 covers the debug agent and dumps.
  2. Does recovery change exception types? → No. The copy has the same class. It changes identity, adds a cause, and changes the stack frames.
  3. Why can't the JVM just keep the stack? → Keeping the stack would mean a stack per coroutine (stackful, like a thread). Kotlin chose stackless coroutines so suspension is cheap and needs no runtime support. The trade-off is losing call history (CPS details are in chunk 13).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "coroutine stack traces are confusing, use the debugger". The senior explains stackless unwinding, @DebugMetadata, copy-with-cause recovery, when it is on (Android needs the property set explicitly), the identity and R8 traps, and a production strategy that doesn't rely on recovery.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A test suite started failing only on CI after a coroutines upgrade, because assertSame(expectedException, actual) saw a recovered copy. JVM tests run with assertions enabled, so debug mode and recovery were on there and nowhere else.

questions.contextHtml: Your team owns a Kotlin-first analytics/feature-flag SDK used by 120 partner apps. Telemetry shows 35% of integrations are Java-only and 40% have minSdk 21-23. The core API is suspend fun fetchFlags(userId: String): Flags. Partners complain they "can't call it". One engineer proposes fun fetchFlagsBlocking(userId: String) = runBlocking { fetchFlags(userId) }. Another proposes exposing only CompletableFuture. A third suggests a third-party compiler plugin that auto-generates blocking bridges. Partner crash reports already show 3 ANRs per 10k sessions traced to an older blocking SDK method being called on main.
questions.promptHtml: How would you design the Java-facing API, and what do you reject?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just add the runBlocking wrapper and tell them to call it on a background thread." Partners will call it on main, and ANRs come back. Or "Use CompletableFuture", which fails at runtime on the 40% below API 24 unless desugaring covers it, and it isn't guaranteed to.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Do partners already ship Guava or RxJava? That decides whether a future type adds dependency weight.
    • Which thread should callbacks be delivered on? Partners expect main for UI, but some want an executor.
    • Do partners need cancellation? Yes, if they fetch per screen.
    • What is the SDK's own lifecycle? Is there an Sdk.shutdown()?
    • How often is it called? This tells me whether caching and deduplication matter more than the shape of the API.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Publish a documented callback-based Java facade in a minor release. Don't ship any blocking variant.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (design options):
    1. A callback interface plus a Cancellable handle, with an optional Executor for delivery. It works on every API level, adds zero deps, and is idiomatic Java. Pick.
    2. A ListenableFuture via kotlinx-coroutines-guava. It's good if partners already use Guava, and it can be offered in an optional -guava artifact.
    3. CompletableFuture via scope.future (core since 1.7). It's fine but limited to API 24+, so it's offered as an extra and is not the only option.
    4. A blocking wrapper. Reject. It recreates the ANR class we already see in partner reports.
    5. A third-party bridge-generating plugin. Reject. It generates blocking bridges, adds build risk, and doesn't solve cancellation.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • A sample Java app per API level (21, 23, 24, 34) in CI.
    • A binary-compatibility validator on the public API.
    • StrictMode in the sample app to catch any main-thread blocking.
    • A test that cancelling the handle cancels the underlying network call (via a fake server with a hanging response).
  5. Root cause (of the partner pain): A suspend function's JVM signature takes a Continuation and returns Object. Java can't call it ergonomically, and the SDK didn't provide a bridge that owns a scope, so partners improvised with blocking calls.
  6. Fix: 
    object FlagsSdk {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate)

    fun interface FlagsCallback { fun onResult(flags: Flags?, error: Throwable?) }
    fun interface Cancellable { fun cancel() }

    @JvmStatic @JvmOverloads
    fun fetchFlags(userId: String, executor: Executor? = null, cb: FlagsCallback): Cancellable {
        val job = scope.launch {
            val r = runCatching { repository.fetchFlags(userId) }   // repository is main-safe internally
            if (r.exceptionOrNull() is CancellationException) return@launch
            val deliver = { cb.onResult(r.getOrNull(), r.exceptionOrNull()) }
            if (executor != null) executor.execute(deliver) else deliver()
        }
        return Cancellable { job.cancel() }
    }

    @JvmStatic fun shutdown() = scope.cancel()
}
    Long-term: keep the suspend API as the primary Kotlin surface, and keep the Java facade as a thin generated-by-hand layer in the same module with tests. Add optional -guava/-jdk artifacts later if partners ask.
  7. Prevention:
    • An API review checklist: "every public suspend function has a Java entry point; no public blocking variant".
    • Binary-compatibility-validator, and lint docs in the Javadoc stating the callback thread.
    • Partner-facing samples in Java.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I wouldn't expose CoroutineScope or Job types to Java partners. That leaks our coroutine version into their API.
    • I wouldn't use GlobalScope. Shutdown and tests would be impossible.
    • I wouldn't deliver callbacks on IO threads by default. Partners would touch UI from it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "What if a partner calls fetchFlags 50 times at startup?" → Deduplicate in-flight requests per userId inside the repository, for example with a shared Deferred guarded by a Mutex (chunk 21 covers the synchronization). The facade stays thin.
  • "A partner says callbacks sometimes arrive after they called cancel." → Cancellation is cooperative. A result computed just before cancel can still be delivered. Check isActive right before delivery, and document "no callback after cancel returns" only if you enforce it, for example by delivering on main and checking a flag on main.
  • "Can Java partners use Kotlin Result?" → Avoid it. Result is an inline class and is awkward from Java. Use a nullable value plus error, or your own sealed result with Java-friendly accessors.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An SDK shipped a getBlocking() "for Java convenience". Within two quarters it was the top ANR frame in three partner apps, and the SDK team got the blame in reviews. The replacement was a callback facade with a cancel handle, plus an emphatic deprecation of the blocking method with @Deprecated(level = ERROR) one major version later.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: proposes runBlocking, or doesn't know the JVM signature problem.
  • Hire: a callback or future facade with an SDK-owned scope, aware of the API 24 CompletableFuture constraint.
  • Strong hire: also cancellation handles, delivery-thread contract, CancellationException filtering, artifacts split by dependency, binary-compat checks, and rejects the alternatives with reasons.

questions.promptHtml: When does resume() run the coroutine's continuation synchronously inside the resumer's call stack, instead of dispatching it, and why does that matter for correctness?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the root of ordering bugs, reentrancy deadlocks and "my StateFlow collector ran before the setter returned" surprises. Few candidates know that resumption can be synchronous.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: resume goes to the DispatchedContinuation, which asks dispatcher.isDispatchNeeded(context). If the answer is false, the continuation runs right there, on the resumer's thread and inside the resumer's stack, before resume() returns. That happens with Dispatchers.Unconfined always, and with Dispatchers.Main.immediate when the resumer is already on the main thread. That second case covers viewModelScope, lifecycleScope and Compose's main-thread work. So code like deferred.complete(x), stateFlow.value = x, or a callback calling cont.resume(x) can run the resumed coroutine's code in the middle of the caller's function, including while the caller holds a lock. With ordinary dispatchers, the resume is just an enqueue.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
caller on MAIN:   fun onDataArrived(x) {
                     synchronized(sdkLock) {
                        pending.resume(x)          // DispatchedContinuation.resumeWith
                           |
                           |-- Main.immediate.isDispatchNeeded() == false (already on main)
                           |-- run inline (through a thread-local event loop)
                           v
                        [resumed coroutine code runs HERE, still holding sdkLock]
                        e.g. calls sdk.nextRequest() -> wants sdkLock -> re-entrant? deadlock?
                     }
                     state = DONE                  // runs AFTER the coroutine's code
                  }

Details:

  • The thread-local event loop. When a resume happens inline, kotlinx.coroutines runs it through an unconfined event loop on that thread. If you're already inside one, nested inline resumes are queued and run after the current one returns, not recursively. That prevents unbounded recursion in chains like A resumes B, which resumes C. It also means the order is "outer first, then queued", which can surprise you.
  • StateFlow with Main.immediate. Setting value on main resumes suspended collectors. Collectors whose context is Main.immediate can run their next iteration before the setter returns. Whether they actually run inline depends on the event loop state. The point is that you can't assume "the setter returns first, then collectors run on a later frame".
  • Dispatchers.Default/IO. isDispatchNeeded is true, so the resume becomes a scheduled task. If the resumer is itself a scheduler worker, the task typically goes into that worker's local queue. It is still asynchronous relative to resume().
  • Dispatchers.Main (non-immediate). It always posts to the Handler. That's the "safe but adds a frame" option.
  • CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED is the same idea at start time: the body runs inline until the first suspension (chunk 15).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Repo {
    private val lock = Any()
    private var waiter: CancellableContinuation<String>? = null

    suspend fun awaitNext(): String = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
        synchronized(lock) { waiter = cont }
    }

    // BROKEN: resumes while holding the lock; with Main.immediate on main, the resumed
    // coroutine runs inside this synchronized block and may call back into Repo.
    fun onMessage(msg: String) = synchronized(lock) {
        waiter?.resume(msg) { _ -> }
        waiter = null
    }

    // CORRECT: take the waiter under the lock, resume outside it
    fun onMessageFixed(msg: String) {
        val w = synchronized(lock) { waiter.also { waiter = null } }
        w?.resume(msg) { _ -> }
    }
}

The resume(value) { onCancellation } overload is the long-standing one. Newer versions add a variant whose lambda also receives the value and context, so check which signature your kotlinx.coroutines version offers.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Resuming continuations, completing CompletableDeferreds or emitting to flows while holding a lock. The resumed code inherits your critical section.
  • Assuming "the line after resume()" runs before the resumed coroutine. That's false under Unconfined and Main.immediate.
  • Using Dispatchers.Unconfined in production to "avoid a thread hop". Code after any suspension then runs on random callback threads (Binder, OkHttp, sensor) with whatever locks they hold.
  • Writing tests with UnconfinedTestDispatcher that pass only because resumption is eager. In production with StandardTestDispatcher-like ordering they fail (testing is chunk 31).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you make a resume always asynchronous? → Resume a coroutine whose context uses a dispatching dispatcher (Dispatchers.Main, Default). Or in your own code, release locks first and then resume. You can't control the resumed coroutine's dispatcher from the resumer side.
  2. Why does viewModelScope use Main.immediate despite these risks? → It avoids a frame of latency and avoids redundant re-dispatch when you're already on main, for example launch from a click handler. That's usually what UI wants. The reentrancy cost is real but rare if you don't resume under locks.
  3. Can inline resumption cause StackOverflowError? → The event loop protects the kotlinx.coroutines paths. But a custom dispatcher that runs blocks inside dispatch (instead of using isDispatchNeeded = false) bypasses it and can recurse deeply.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "resume puts the coroutine back on its dispatcher." The senior explains isDispatchNeeded, which dispatchers resume inline, the unconfined event loop's queueing semantics, the "resume under lock" reentrancy hazard, and the release-then-resume discipline.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Bluetooth wrapper resumed a waiting coroutine inside its GATT callback lock. On Main.immediate paths the resumed coroutine issued the next write, which needed the same non-reentrant lock, and it froze. Scenario Q277 walks through that incident.

questions.promptHtml: What does a suspension cost in allocations and CPU? When does it actually matter, and what can you do about it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Coroutines are cheap" is true but incomplete. A senior should be able to say what gets allocated, what the compiler already optimizes, and when a hot path should avoid suspension or avoid per-item launch/withContext.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A suspend function that has real suspension points allocates one continuation object (its state machine) per invocation, holding the label, spilled locals and the completion reference. That object is reused across all of that call's suspensions. A suspension that actually parks adds more: library primitives such as suspendCancellableCoroutine allocate a CancellableContinuationImpl, the dispatcher path uses a DispatchedContinuation (cached on the continuation), and delay also allocates a timer task. A suspend call that returns immediately still paid the continuation allocation. The compiler skips the state machine for functions whose only suspend call is in tail position. The cost is tens of bytes and tens of nanoseconds per call, so it is irrelevant for network or disk work, and it matters in tight loops with millions of calls, such as per-element withContext, per-item launch, or tiny suspend functions called in a hot path.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
What allocates, in order of how often it happens (sizes are my estimates and vary by JVM/ART and by number of spilled locals; measure before quoting numbers):

Event Allocation Notes
Call to a suspend function with >= 1 non-tail suspension point 1 ContinuationImpl subclass instance Fields: label, result, spilled locals (L$0, I$0...), completion. Roughly 32-64 bytes.
Same function re-entered after resume none The prologue checks if (cont is MyFun$1 && (cont.label and MIN_VALUE) != 0) and reuses the existing object.
Suspend function whose only suspend call is in tail position none (tail-call optimization) Compiler just forwards the caller's continuation.
suspendCancellableCoroutine 1 CancellableContinuationImpl (+ optional handle for invokeOnCancellation) Plus the interception wrapper cached once per state machine.
Resume via dispatcher DispatchedContinuation is created by intercepted() and cached; it doubles as the task object No extra Runnable per hop in the common path.
delay(n) continuation + a scheduled task node On Android Main, a Handler.postDelayed message.
launch/async the coroutine object (StandaloneCoroutine/DeferredCoroutine), its JobSupport state, the suspend-lambda instance, a context object when + creates a new combined context Several objects, perhaps 150-300 bytes in total.
withContext(sameDispatcher) a ScopeCoroutine-like object; no dispatch Fast path avoids thread hop but still creates objects.
withContext(otherDispatcher) the above + a dispatch hop (queue insert, possible thread wake-up) Real latency: microseconds, not nanoseconds.

Why it rarely matters: one network call costs milliseconds and a continuation costs nanoseconds, a difference of five or six orders of magnitude. Allocation is short-lived (young generation), and ART's generational GC handles it cheaply.

When it does matter:

  1. Hot loops with per-element suspension. Example: items.forEach { launch { process(it) } } for 500k items, or for (x in list) withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { f(x) }. You pay launch/dispatch overhead per element. Batch instead: one withContext outside the loop, or chunk the list into core-count pieces.
  2. Tiny suspend functions on the critical path. A suspend fun isEnabled(): Boolean that usually returns from an in-memory cache is allocated on each call. Keep a non-suspend fast path and a suspend slow path.
  3. Flow pipelines. Every operator adds a collector object, and every emission is a suspend call. Per-element overhead matters at hundreds of thousands of items per second (chunk 24 and 28 cover the operator costs).
  4. GC and jank. Allocation churn in a frame loop (scroll bind, gesture handling) can add young-GC pauses. Measure with Perfetto and the Android Studio memory profiler's allocation tracking.

Fast-path pattern:

class FlagCache(private val remote: RemoteFlags) {
    private val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Boolean>()

    // Non-suspend hot path: zero continuation allocation
    fun peek(key: String): Boolean? = cache[key]

    // Suspend path only when truly needed
    suspend fun get(key: String): Boolean =
        cache[key] ?: remote.fetch(key).also { cache[key] = it }
}

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Wasteful: dispatch + coroutine overhead per element
suspend fun sumSquaresSlow(xs: IntArray): Long = xs.fold(0L) { acc, x ->
    acc + withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { x.toLong() * x }   // 1M dispatch hops
}

// Better: one switch, plain loop inside
suspend fun sumSquares(xs: IntArray): Long = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
    var acc = 0L
    for (x in xs) acc += x.toLong() * x
    acc
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting "a coroutine costs ~1 KB" or "a few bytes" without measuring. Real numbers depend on the lambda captures and spilled locals.
  • Optimizing allocation in code that makes a network call anyway.
  • Marking a suspend function that never really suspends as suspend just in case, then calling it in a tight loop. Not suspending is cheap, but not free.
  • Assuming inline on a suspend function removes the state machine. Inlined suspend bodies join the caller's state machine, which removes the callee's continuation, but only for inline functions with lambda parameters you can inline.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you measure it? → A Microbenchmark (androidx.benchmark) comparing the loop variants, with allocation counts from the benchmark output. On the JVM, JMH with the GC profiler. Don't trust a stopwatch around a loop.
  2. What is the tail-call optimization exactly? → If the last action of a suspend function is a call to another suspend function whose result is returned directly, the compiler can pass its own continuation through and skip creating a state machine. It is a compiler optimization, not a guarantee in all cases (for example, the call inside try or with post-processing is not a tail call).
  3. Why not just make everything non-suspend and block? → Because blocking costs a whole thread (about 1 MB reserved stack per platform thread by default on JVM, less on Android configurations) and 10k blocked threads is not feasible, while 10k suspended coroutines are a few MB of heap. The allocation per suspension is the price of that.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "coroutines are lightweight". The senior names which objects exist per call, per suspension and per hop, the tail-call and continuation-reuse optimizations, the cases where the cost shows up (per-element dispatch, flow hot paths, frame loops), and the rule to measure with a benchmark rather than guess.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed screen's list diffing used withContext(Default) per item to "parallelize" 3,000-item comparisons. The scheduling overhead exceeded the work, and moving to one withContext with a plain loop cut p95 diff time from about 180 ms to about 25 ms on a mid-range device (illustrative composite figures).

questions.contextHtml:
A ride-hailing app (4M DAU) has a FareEstimator that caches estimates per route. A recent PR "made it thread-safe" with a ReentrantLock. Crashlytics shows IllegalMonitorStateException: attempt to unlock lock, not locked by current thread at 0.4% of sessions, plus a rarer pattern of the estimate screen freezing forever (about 30 reports per week) with all DefaultDispatcher-worker threads parked. The red herring: the crash started the same week as an OkHttp upgrade.

class FareEstimator(private val api: FareApi) {
    private val lock = ReentrantLock()
    private val cache = HashMap<String, Fare>()

    suspend fun estimate(route: String): Fare {
        lock.lock()
        try {
            cache[route]?.let { return it }
            val fare = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { api.fetch(route) }   // suspension point
            cache[route] = fare
            return fare
        } finally {
            lock.unlock()
        }
    }
}

Callers: viewModelScope.launch { _fare.value = estimator.estimate(route) } from several screens, on Dispatchers.Main.immediate.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs, explain why they only appear in production, and fix it properly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use synchronized instead" (the compiler rejects suspension inside synchronized), or "put @Volatile on the map". It also misses that the lock is owned by a thread and the coroutine moves between threads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Which thread calls estimate first? It is main (from viewModelScope), which matters for the freeze.
    • How long does api.fetch take at p95? If 800 ms, then every other caller is blocked on main for that long.
    • Is the cache correctness requirement "one fetch per route" or just "no corruption"? It decides between a mutex and a deduplicating map.
    • Does anything else call lock? Rules out lock-order issues.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that removes the ReentrantLock and guards the map with a coroutine Mutex (see fix). Roll back the PR if the hotfix needs more than a day.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. A thread-owned lock is acquired on one thread and released on another after the suspension. This explains IllegalMonitorStateException on unlock().
    2. A second caller on Main calls lock.lock() while the first is suspended in withContext. lock() blocks the main thread until the fetch completes, and since the first coroutine's continuation resumes on Main.immediate, it needs the main thread to resume. The main thread is stuck in lock(): deadlock (freeze/ANR).
    3. OkHttp upgrade. A red herring: the exceptions come from our own code and the stack frames show FareEstimator.
    4. Cache HashMap corruption. Possible but secondary, since the lock was meant to protect it.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Read the IllegalMonitorStateException stack: it is raised from lock.unlock() in FareEstimator.estimate.
    • Read the ANR/freeze main-thread stack: ReentrantLock.lock → LockSupport.park on main.
    • Reproduce in a test with a single-threaded Main replacement and two concurrent estimate calls; with runTest and a fake FareApi that suspends on a CompletableDeferred.
    • Check Perfetto/thread dump for the lock owner field to confirm the owner thread differs from the unlocking thread.
  5. Root cause: ReentrantLock is owned by a thread. A coroutine is not a thread. After withContext(Dispatchers.IO) suspends and resumes, the coroutine continues on a different thread (an IO worker, then possibly Main again), so the finally calls unlock() from a thread that doesn't hold the lock, hence the exception. Meanwhile the original owner thread (Main) has moved on and still holds the lock from the lock's point of view, and a second lock() call blocks that thread. When the blocked thread is Main and the first coroutine's continuation needs Main to finish, the app deadlocks. (Kotlin rejects suspension points inside a synchronized block at compile time for exactly this reason. ReentrantLock has no such compile-time check.)
  6. Fix: Short-term: use a coroutine Mutex, which suspends instead of blocking and isn't owned by a thread. 
    class FareEstimator(private val api: FareApi) {
    private val mutex = Mutex()
    private val cache = HashMap<String, Fare>()

    suspend fun estimate(route: String): Fare = mutex.withLock {
        cache[route] ?: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { api.fetch(route) }.also { cache[route] = it }
    }
}
    Mutex is not reentrant, so don't call estimate recursively from inside it. (Mutex deep-dive is chunk 21.) Long-term: a single global mutex serializes different routes. Better is per-route deduplication: 
    private val inFlight = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Deferred<Fare>>()
suspend fun estimate(route: String): Fare = coroutineScope {
    val d = inFlight.getOrPut(route) { async(Dispatchers.IO) { api.fetch(route) } }
    try { d.await() } finally { if (d.isCompleted) inFlight.remove(route, d) }
}
    This is a sketch. A production version needs care with cancellation of the shared async and its scope (the deferred should live in an owner scope, not the first caller's). Alternatively keep a StateFlow-backed cache or a library like a Store.
  7. Prevention:
    • Detekt/lint rule that flags ReentrantLock.lock(), Semaphore.acquire() (java.util.concurrent), Object.wait() and Thread.sleep() inside suspend functions.
    • Review checklist: "critical sections that contain suspension points use Mutex; critical sections without suspension may use synchronized."
    • A concurrency test: two parallel calls with a fake API that suspends.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I would not wrap the whole body in runBlocking to keep the lock logic. It deadlocks Main even faster.
    • I would not simply move callers to Dispatchers.IO. The IllegalMonitorStateException remains, because the thread still changes after the suspension.
    • I would not use synchronized around only the map access and keep the fetch outside. That is actually valid and often best if "duplicate fetches are acceptable". It's the cheapest fix when dedup is not required.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why does Kotlin forbid suspension inside synchronized but allow it inside lock.withLock { }?" → synchronized is an inline function over monitor enter/exit bytecode, and the compiler has a specific check for suspension points in a monitor region. ReentrantLock.withLock is an ordinary inline function over library calls, so the compiler has no way to know that it is a critical section.
  • "Is Mutex.withLock safe if the coroutine is cancelled while waiting?" → Yes. lock() is cancellable, and withLock releases in a finally if it acquired. A cancelled waiter never acquires.
  • "What if the mutex holder is cancelled mid-fetch?" → withLock releases the mutex. The cache just wasn't written. The next caller refetches.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team ported a Java singleton full of synchronized methods into suspend functions by adding suspend and swapping to ReentrantLock. It passed review, passed tests (single-threaded runTest), and deadlocked on real devices because two screens triggered it at once from Main. The Mutex rewrite was five lines, and the test was one async pair with a hanging fake.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests volatile or "retry on exception", doesn't see the thread-ownership issue.
  • Hire: identifies thread-owned lock across a suspension, explains the unlock exception and the Main deadlock, uses Mutex.
  • Strong hire: also explains why synchronized is rejected at compile time, designs per-key deduplication with correct scope ownership, notes Mutex non-reentrancy, and adds lint plus a deterministic concurrency test.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app (900k DAU) has a legacy analytics tracker with Tracker.setSession(id) backed by a ThreadLocal<String>. Every event reads Tracker.currentSession(). Last sprint the networking and repository layers moved to coroutines running on Dispatchers.IO. Data team reports that 2.1% of events carry another user-session's ID (mostly in the first minute after login on shared tablets in a retail partner's stores), and funnel numbers are inconsistent. Unit tests pass. A teammate says the red herring: "the backend must be mixing up sessions", because the same bug did not show in iOS. Code:

class CheckoutRepo(private val api: Api, private val tracker: Tracker) {
    suspend fun submit(cart: Cart) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        tracker.track("checkout_started")           // reads ThreadLocal
        val r = api.submit(cart)                    // suspends
        tracker.track("checkout_done")              // reads ThreadLocal again
        r
    }
}
// somewhere at login
Tracker.setSession(session.id)                       // called on Main
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose the wrong session IDs and design a fix that does not require rewriting every call site at once.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Blame the backend or add synchronization around the tracker". Another weak answer: "Call setSession before every track call", which hides the problem and races under load.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Where was the ThreadLocal set, and on which thread? The login code sets it on Main only; IO workers never have it.
    • Do wrong IDs belong to real other sessions, or are they null/default? If real, then it's thread reuse; if null, it was never set on that thread.
    • Do we have multiple sessions alive at once (shared tablet with quick user switch)? That explains the retail pattern.
    • How many coroutine dispatchers do we use for events? It sizes the migration.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop reading the ThreadLocal directly in the coroutine paths. Pass the session ID explicitly into track() in the three highest-volume flows. Add a server-side filter to quarantine events where the client session doesn't match the auth token.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. A ThreadLocal value is bound to the thread, while the coroutine hops threads, and pool workers get reused by other coroutines that belong to other sessions. This fits "wrong, real session ID".
    2. A race between login setSession on Main and early IO events that read before it is set. This fits "null or previous user's value right after login".
    3. Backend mixing sessions. It's a red herring, because the app sends the wrong ID and the server faithfully records it, and iOS has no ThreadLocal.
    4. Unit tests pass because they run on a single thread, where the ThreadLocal is consistent.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Add a debug log of Thread.currentThread().name plus session in track, and see the same coroutine reading different values across the suspension.
    • Write a repro with two coroutines on a 2-thread dispatcher with different sessions and delays in between.
    • Compare event session IDs with auth-token user IDs server-side to count mismatches.
    • Confirm iOS differences are due to the platform, not backend.
  5. Root cause: ThreadLocal state is attached to a thread. The IO pool has dozens of reusable workers. After api.submit(cart) suspends, the coroutine resumes on whichever worker is free, so tracker.track("checkout_done") reads that worker's ThreadLocal, which may be unset or set by earlier work that belongs to another session. The unit tests used one thread and so could not show it.
  6. Fix: Short-term, propagate the value with the coroutine context so it follows the coroutine: 
    object Tracker {
    private val session = ThreadLocal<String?>()
    fun currentSession(): String? = session.get()
    fun sessionContext(id: String) = session.asContextElement(id)
}

class SessionHolder { @Volatile var current: String? = null }

// Put the element on the scope that runs this user's work
val userScope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate + Tracker.sessionContext(session.id))
    Every coroutine started from userScope (and withContext(Dispatchers.IO), which inherits context) now has the ThreadLocal set on every resume and restored on every suspension. On user switch, cancel the old scope and create a new one with the new ID. Long-term: pass sessionId explicitly, or inject a SessionProvider into the tracker. Context elements are good for logging/tracing glue and not for business logic. Use ensurePresent() in Tracker entry points used from coroutines to fail fast in debug builds when the element is missing.
  7. Prevention:
    • A test with a two-thread dispatcher and interleaved delays that asserts the session at both track points.
    • Lint rule or review rule: no new ThreadLocal for request or user scoped state in coroutine code.
    • Server-side validation that the event's session matches the authenticated user, with an alert on mismatch rate above 0.1%.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I would not switch everything to a single-thread dispatcher to make the ThreadLocal "work". It hides the bug, serializes IO, and still breaks the first time someone adds Dispatchers.Default.
    • I would not call Tracker.setSession inside the coroutine. set() inside a coroutine isn't preserved across suspensions.
    • I would not keep the global ThreadLocal as the source of truth after the migration. It is a bridge, not a design.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "The element is on the scope but one event still has the wrong ID." → Check code that runs outside coroutines on pool threads (a legacy executor callback). It never gets the element. Also check any GlobalScope.launch or a manually created scope without the element.
  • "What about Dispatchers.Main.immediate edge cases?" → Context elements are applied around inline execution too, but there are reported edge cases (kotlinx.coroutines issue #4121) where a value lingers on the thread. Don't rely on ThreadLocals for security-sensitive decisions.
  • "Could we use CopyableThreadContextElement?" → Only if children need a derived copy (for example a mutable span stack). Here the immutable ID is simple. That API is experimental, so check the opt-in on your version.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: On a migration where logs showed another user's request ID, the culprit was an MDC-style ThreadLocal. The fix was a one-line MDCContext() equivalent on the base scope. The more valuable lesson was that the tests all used a single-threaded test dispatcher, so the team started running concurrency tests on a 4-thread dispatcher by default.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames backend/network, or adds more setSession calls.
  • Hire: explains thread hopping and worker reuse, uses asContextElement on the owning scope, and knows set() inside the coroutine won't persist.
  • Strong hire: also proposes explicit parameter passing as the long-term fix, adds ensurePresent and a multi-threaded repro test, handles user switching by scope replacement, and adds server-side mismatch detection.

questions.contextHtml:
A BLE medical-device app (150k devices, p95 session 25 minutes) wraps a GATT client in a coroutine API. Since release 8.2, about 0.9% of sessions freeze: the UI stops responding for 5+ seconds, then Play reports an ANR (rate moved from 0.12% to 0.55%). It happens mostly when users tap "sync" immediately after connecting. Main-thread ANR trace:

"main" prio=5 tid=1 Blocked
  - waiting to lock <0x0a1b2c3d> (a java.lang.Object) held by thread 1 (main)   // (shown on API 30 as self-owned monitor re-entrance attempt via wrapper)
  at com.app.ble.GattBridge.writeNext(GattBridge.kt:58)
  at com.app.ble.SyncUseCase$run$1.invokeSuspend(SyncUseCase.kt:34)
  at kotlinx.coroutines.DispatchedTask.run(DispatchedTask.kt:...)
  at com.app.ble.GattBridge$callback$1.onCharacteristicWrite(GattBridge.kt:41)

Some devices show a frozen non-reentrant custom lock instead of a Java monitor. Another team suspects the BLE stack firmware (red herring, since devices on firmware 2.1 and 2.3 both fail). Code:

class GattBridge(private val gatt: BluetoothGatt) {
    private val lock = Any()
    private var pending: CancellableContinuation<Unit>? = null

    suspend fun writeNext(chunk: ByteArray) {
        suspendCancellableCoroutine<Unit> { cont ->
            synchronized(lock) { pending = cont }
            gatt.writeCharacteristic(chunk)          // simplified
        }
    }

    val callback = object : BluetoothGattCallback() {
        override fun onCharacteristicWrite(g: BluetoothGatt, c: BluetoothGattCharacteristic, status: Int) {
            synchronized(lock) {
                pending?.resume(Unit)               // runs the coroutine's next step inline on Main.immediate
                pending = null
            }
        }
    }
}

The sync use case loops for (chunk in chunks) bridge.writeNext(chunk) in viewModelScope (Main.immediate), and the GATT callback is delivered on the main thread on this app's target setup.
questions.promptHtml: Why does it freeze, why only sometimes, and how do you fix it without risking BLE ordering?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Blame the BLE firmware or add a timeout". A timeout hides the symptom. Another weak answer is "make the lock a ReentrantLock", which masks the reentrancy without addressing resume-under-lock and the stale pending = null.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Which thread delivers onCharacteristicWrite? On this setup it is Main, so Main.immediate resumes inline.
    • Does the freeze correlate with devices that complete the write callback synchronously or very fast? Yes, "tap sync right after connect" suggests fast callbacks on a warm connection.
    • Is it a hard deadlock or an infinite loop? The trace is a blocked monitor or a custom lock, not CPU spinning.
    • Does the bug exist on firmware that completes writes slower? It reproduces on both, so firmware isn't the variable.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side kill switch to disable chunked sync in favour of the old blocking path for affected app versions, and a hotfix with the fix below. Extend the existing ANR dashboard with a per-version split to confirm.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Resuming the continuation while holding lock runs the next loop iteration (writeNext) inline inside the callback, which tries to take lock again, and with a non-reentrant primitive (or with a stale pending overwritten) this stalls. This matches the stack: onCharacteristicWrite appears below invokeSuspend and writeNext.
    2. pending = null after the inline resume erases the new continuation that the inline writeNext just registered, so the next write's completion has nobody to resume. That is a hang rather than a deadlock, and it is a second bug in the same code path.
    3. BLE firmware. A red herring: reproduces on two firmware versions and the stack is entirely in our code.
    4. Main thread being busy elsewhere. Possible background, but the trace shows lock-related blocking.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Read the trace order: callback → DispatchedTask.run → invokeSuspend → writeNext. This proves inline resumption (no dispatcher hop).
    • Reproduce with a fake BluetoothGatt that calls the callback synchronously from writeCharacteristic, in a Robolectric or plain JVM test with a Main.immediate-like test dispatcher.
    • Add logging around pending to catch the overwrite.
    • Use the coroutine debug agent in a debug build, and dump coroutines to see which are suspended on writeNext with no pending to resume.
  5. Root cause: Two coupled mistakes. First, resume was called while holding a lock, and Main.immediate ran the resumed coroutine inline in the resumer's call stack (Q273), so the next writeNext ran inside the critical section. Second, the code cleared pending after the resume, so it wiped the continuation registered by the inline re-entry, causing a lost wake-up. The first fails fast when the lock is non-reentrant. A Java monitor is reentrant on the same thread, so there the second bug shows up as a silent hang.
  6. Fix: Short-term: take the continuation out under the lock, release the lock, then resume. Never resume under a lock. 
    override fun onCharacteristicWrite(g: BluetoothGatt, c: BluetoothGattCharacteristic, status: Int) {
    val cont = synchronized(lock) { pending.also { pending = null } }   // clear BEFORE resuming
    if (status == BluetoothGatt.GATT_SUCCESS) cont?.resume(Unit)
    else cont?.resumeWithException(IOException("GATT write failed: $status"))
}
    Also register cancellation, and make the registration atomic with the write: 
    suspend fun writeNext(chunk: ByteArray) = suspendCancellableCoroutine<Unit> { cont ->
    synchronized(lock) { check(pending == null) { "write already in flight" }; pending = cont }
    cont.invokeOnCancellation { synchronized(lock) { if (pending === cont) pending = null } }
    if (!gatt.writeCharacteristic(chunk)) {      // simplified API
        synchronized(lock) { pending = null }
        cont.resumeWithException(IOException("write rejected"))
    }
}
    Long-term: model the GATT operation queue as a Channel of operations processed by a single coroutine (chunk 22), so ordering is enforced structurally. The callback only does trySend of results, which is a non-blocking handoff and cannot run user code inline.
  7. Prevention:
    • Rule: "never resume a continuation, complete a CompletableDeferred or emit to a flow while holding a lock".
    • A fake-GATT test with synchronous callbacks, and a test with delayed callbacks.
    • The check(pending == null) guard turns silent lost wake-ups into loud failures in debug.
    • ANR alert split by app version, and a staged rollout gate on ANR rate (0.47% bad-behavior threshold in Play vitals).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I would not switch the sync loop to Dispatchers.Main (non-immediate) as the only fix. It hides the reentrancy by adding a hop, but the pending = null ordering bug remains for other dispatchers' interleavings.
    • I would not add a timeout as the fix. It converts a deadlock into a slow error and leaves BLE state inconsistent.
    • I would not use Dispatchers.Unconfined to "match" the callback thread. It makes the inline-resume problem worse.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why does the freeze not occur if the callback comes slowly?" → When the write completes later, writeNext has already suspended and returned from invokeSuspend, and the lock is not held by anyone upstream. Fast or synchronous callbacks complete before the first call has finished registering, so the resumption nests.
  • "What if writeCharacteristic invokes the callback synchronously before returning?" → Then resume happens inside suspendCancellableCoroutine's block. That is allowed: the continuation resumes before suspension is finalized, and the fast path returns the value without suspending (Q267). The pending bookkeeping must tolerate that.
  • "How would you test the fix deterministically?" → A fake gatt that gives you control: writeCharacteristic enqueues, and the test calls callback.onCharacteristicWrite at chosen moments, including inside writeCharacteristic itself. Run on UnconfinedTestDispatcher and StandardTestDispatcher to cover both resumption modes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A device-sync feature flaked for months with "BLE is unreliable" as the accepted explanation. The actual cause was a resume under a lock that only manifested when the OS delivered the callback inline. After the fix and an operation queue, the ANR rate returned to baseline and the "unreliable BLE" tickets stopped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: attributes it to firmware or adds a timeout, doesn't connect the stack order to inline resumption.
  • Hire: identifies resume-under-lock with Main.immediate inline execution, and fixes by resuming outside the lock.
  • Strong hire: also finds the pending = null lost wake-up bug, handles cancellation and rejected writes, proposes a Channel-based operation queue, and writes deterministic tests for both inline and delayed callbacks.
